Work from the project root, the main folder of the course. Read each step before you run its R chunk. All data are simulated. These exercises cannot show a finding about a real disease.

The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the course words. Each module reads its input files from disk. You do not need a saved R workspace.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
setwd(start_dir)
```

## Module 7 at a glance {#module-7-overview}

**What you will do.** You will turn the results of the association test into plots and tables. You will check that the results are trustworthy. Then you will find the strong signals and write a short report.

**What you will learn.**

- How to draw and read the two main GWAS plots.
- How to check if the test results are too strong overall.
- How to choose a p-value threshold when you run many tests.
- How to group nearby signals and look closely at one region.
- How to report results honestly, including their limits.

**How long it takes.** About 75 minutes. The slowest step is 7.7, because PLINK runs two new association scans.

## 7.1 QQ plot {#step-7-1}

### What we do

Draw a QQ plot. It compares the p-values we observed with the p-values we would expect if no variant were linked to the disease. We use only the [autosomal](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) variants, on chromosomes 1 to 22.

The plot reads the [summary statistics file](../docs/glossary.md#summary-statistics) that we made at step 6.8. This file is a table with one row for each tested variant. Each row holds the chromosome, the position, the alleles, the odds ratio, the standard error, the p-value and the number of samples. The plots in this module all read this one file, so every figure comes from the same results.

### Why

A [QQ plot](../docs/glossary.md#qq-plot) puts the observed p-values in order and pairs each one with the value that we expect by chance. If no variant is linked to the disease, the [p-values](../docs/glossary.md#p-value) are spread evenly between 0 and 1. The plot shows -log10 of each p-value. This turns small p-values into large positive numbers, so strong results appear high on the plot.

If the tests behave well, the points follow the diagonal line. A few strong associations lift only the highest points at the right end. A wider departure along the whole line can have several causes: [confounding](../docs/glossary.md#confounding), technical problems, a wrong model or many true small effects. The picture alone cannot tell these causes apart. Nearby variants can be correlated through [linkage disequilibrium (LD)](../docs/glossary.md#ld), so the points are not fully independent.

### You need

The summary statistics file from step 6.8. If R says that the file is missing, run step 6.8 first.

### Command

```{r s7-1}
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
autosomal <- stats$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.1", "qq.png"), function() plot_qq(stats$p_value[autosomal], "Adjusted simulated GWAS: autosomal QQ plot"))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Most points are close to the diagonal line. The highest points at the right end leave the line strongly. Missing, zero or invalid p-values are not drawn as if they were strong results. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

```{r s7-1_expected_figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Most adjusted autosomal tests follow the null diagonal, with an upper-tail departure from a few association signals."}
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "7.1", "qq.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does a strong departure only at the highest points always mean confounding across the whole genome?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. A few true signals can lift the highest points while most other tests stay close to the line.

</details>

### Files created

`s7-1_qq.png`.

## 7.2 Genomic inflation factor {#step-7-2}

### What we do

Calculate lambda for the autosomal variants. Then read it together with the QQ plot.

### Why

The genomic inflation factor, [lambda](../docs/glossary.md#lambda-gc), is one number that tells if the p-values are too small overall. This problem is called [inflation](../docs/glossary.md#inflation). We calculate lambda in three steps. First, we convert each valid p-value into a [chi-square statistic](../docs/glossary.md#chi-square-statistic). Second, we take the [median](../docs/glossary.md#median) of these statistics, the middle value after sorting. Third, we divide this median by the value expected by chance, which is approximately 0.4549.

A lambda near one means that the middle of the results looks as expected. It does not prove that there is no confounding. Lambda also depends on the sample size, on how many variants have small true effects, on the model and on the set of variants tested. Do not divide every test by lambda without thinking. Do not treat one cut-off as a simple pass or fail.

### You need

The same autosomal p-values that we used at 7.1. R reads them from the summary statistics file made at step 6.8.

### Command

```{r s7-2}
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
p <- stats$p_value[stats$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)]
lambda <- lambda_gc(p)
print(lambda)
stopifnot(abs(lambda - 1.016) < 0.001)
guided_write(data.frame(model = "QC plus ten PCs", lambda = lambda), guided_path(cfg, "7.2", "lambda.tsv"))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Lambda is approximately 1.016. R calculates it from the valid autosomal tests.

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Can a lambda near one prove that a particular top variant is causal?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Lambda summarises the middle of all the tests. It does not show that one single association is valid or causal.

</details>

### Files created

`s7-2_lambda.tsv`.

## 7.3 Manhattan plot {#step-7-3}

### What we do

Draw a Manhattan plot of the association results along the autosomes. The plot reads the summary statistics file made at step 6.8.

### Why

A [Manhattan plot](../docs/glossary.md#manhattan-plot) shows every tested variant as one point. The horizontal axis shows the chromosome and the position. The vertical axis shows -log10(p), so stronger results are higher. Nearby high points are often correlated through LD, so they may be one single signal. The position tells us where the evidence is, not which gene causes the effect.

All positions use the [GRCh38](../docs/glossary.md#grch38) genome build. The plot gives alternate chromosomes different colours. The chromosome labels and the order of the positions give the same information, so colour is not the only clue.

### You need

The summary statistics file from step 6.8. If R says that the file is missing, run step 6.8 first.

### Command

```{r s7-3}
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
plot_data <- data.frame(CHROM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(stats$chromosome)),
  POS = stats$base_pair_location, P = stats$p_value)
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan.png"), function() plot_manhattan(plot_data, "Simulated GWAS: age, sex and ten PCs"))
stopifnot(sum(stats$p_value[valid_p(stats$p_value)] < 5e-8) == 8L)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

There are three strong regions, on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12. Together they hold eight variants below 5e-8. The moderate region that we planted does not reach this usual threshold. Tests on the sex chromosomes and MT stay in the result table, but this figure shows only the autosomes. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

```{r s7-3_expected_figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Autosomal association peaks exceed the conventional threshold on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12."}
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Do four nearby significant variants always mean four independent causal effects?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Because of LD, several tested variants can point to the same single signal.

</details>

## 7.4 Multiple-testing thresholds {#step-7-4}

### What we do

Compare three ways to decide which p-values are small enough to call a result: the usual GWAS threshold, a Bonferroni threshold for this scan and a false-discovery-rate adjustment.

### Why

Running many tests at once is called [multiple testing](../docs/glossary.md#multiple-testing). Every test has a small chance of a false positive, so many tests give many chances. The [Bonferroni correction](../docs/glossary.md#bonferroni) handles this simply. We choose an error rate alpha, for example 0.05. We divide it by the number of tests. The result is the p-value threshold. This keeps the chance of even one false positive at or below alpha, also when the tests are correlated.

The usual GWAS threshold is 5e-8, which means 0.00000005. It is called [genome-wide significance](../docs/glossary.md#genome-wide-significance). It is about 0.05 divided by one million common-variant tests. It is a convention. It is not a guarantee for every ancestry, every study design or every set of tests.

The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method controls a different quantity. This quantity is the [false discovery rate](../docs/glossary.md#false-discovery-rate), the expected share of false results among the results that we call significant. Decide which tests belong to the family before you look at the results.

### You need

The valid additive results from the summary statistics file made at step 6.8. Do not replace p-values that failed with other values.

### Command

```{r s7-4}
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
p <- stats$p_value[valid_p(stats$p_value)]
threshold <- data.frame(rule = c("Conventional GWAS", "Bonferroni for this scan", "BH adjusted p at 0.05"),
  threshold = c(5e-8, 0.05 / length(p), 0.05),
  discoveries = c(sum(p < 5e-8), sum(p < 0.05 / length(p)), sum(p.adjust(p, method = "BH") < 0.05)))
print(threshold)
guided_write(threshold, guided_path(cfg, "7.4", "thresholds.tsv"))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

There are 236,815 finite tests, so the Bonferroni threshold for this scan is approximately 2.11e-7. The usual threshold gives eight discoveries. BH answers a different question about errors, so it can return more.

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does a false discovery rate of 5% mean that each reported variant has a 5% chance of being false?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The rate describes the whole set of discoveries on average. It is not a probability for each single variant.

</details>

### Files created

`s7-4_thresholds.tsv`.

## 7.5 Clump correlated results {#step-7-5}

### What we do

Group significant variants that are correlated into clumps. Each clump has one top variant. We measure the correlation in our own cohort.

### Why

[Clumping](../docs/glossary.md#clumping) starts with the variant that has the smallest p-value. This is the [lead variant](../docs/glossary.md#lead-variant), also called the index variant. PLINK adds the nearby variants that are correlated with it. Then PLINK takes the next smallest p-value that is still free and repeats the process. The result is a list of regions that are approximately independent. The settings for the distance and the correlation decide what counts as a region.

Clumping is not [fine-mapping](../docs/glossary.md#fine-mapping). It does not show causes, and it does not prove one causal effect in each clump. Measure the correlation in the cohort that you analysed, not in an external population that does not match.

### You need

The full genotype set from step 5.7 and the PLINK association report from step 6.4, unchanged. This step still reads the PLINK report and not the summary statistics file. The reason is that the `--clump` option of PLINK expects the format of its own report.

### Command

```{r s7-5}
report <- guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--clump", paste0(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"), ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"),
  "--clump-id-field", "ID", "--clump-p-field", "P", "--clump-p1", "5e-8", "--clump-p2", "1e-5",
  "--clump-r2", "0.1", "--clump-kb", "250", "--clump-unphased", "--out", report))
clumps <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".clumps"))
print(clumps)
stopifnot(nrow(clumps) == 3L)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --clump results/guided/s6-4_association.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid --clump-id-field ID --clump-p-field P --clump-p1 5e-8 --clump-p2 1e-5 --clump-r2 0.1 --clump-kb 250 --clump-unphased --out results/guided/s7-5_clump --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--clump` reads the association report. `--clump-id-field ID` names the column that holds the variant ID. `--clump-p-field P` names the column that holds the p-value. `--clump-p1 5e-8` sets the p-value that a variant needs to be a lead variant. `--clump-p2 1e-5` sets the p-value that other variants need to be listed in a clump. `--clump-r2 0.1` sets the [r^2](../docs/glossary.md#r-squared) threshold: a variant joins a clump only if its squared correlation with the lead is above 0.1. `--clump-kb 250` sets the distance limit in kilobases (250 kb on each side of the lead). `--clump-unphased` uses the squared correlation of the genotype dosages, so the definition of LD is clear. `--pfile` reads the genotype files in the PLINK 2 format. `--out` names the report. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory in MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

There are three clumps. They describe the strong regions on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12. The report gives the ID and the p-value of each lead variant. This does not show that there are three causal variants.

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

If we change the LD threshold or the distance, can the clumps change even though the association scan stays the same?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Yes. The clumps depend on these settings and on the samples used to measure LD.

</details>

### Files created

`s7-5_clump.clumps` and the log files.

## 7.6 Regional plot {#step-7-6}

### What we do

Look closely at the L2 region. Each variant is coloured by its LD with the lead variant of the region.

### Why

A [regional plot](../docs/glossary.md#regional-plot) shows a small part of the genome. It shows three things together: the position, the strength of the association and the LD. We use L2, on chromosome 9. We do not use L1, because L1 has only one genome-wide significant variant in this set of array variants.

Nearby points with a high r^2 to the lead variant can carry the same association signal. Low LD, or several separate peaks, do not by themselves show several causal effects. We do not name genes and we do not add any other annotation here.

### You need

The summary statistics file from step 6.8, the final cohort and the lead variant 9:96426973:A:G from the clump on chromosome 9.

### Command

```{r s7-6}
lead <- "9:96426973:A:G"
report <- guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "ld")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--chr", "9", "--from-bp", "95926973", "--to-bp", "96926973",
  "--r2-unphased", "--ld-snp", lead, "--ld-window-kb", "500", "--ld-window-r2", "0", "--out", report))
ld <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".vcor"))
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
region <- stats[stats$chromosome == "9" & abs(stats$base_pair_location - 96426973) <= 500000 & valid_p(stats$p_value), ]
r2_column <- grep("R2$", names(ld), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(r2_column) == 1L)
r2 <- as.numeric(ld[[r2_column]][match(region$variant_id, ld$ID_B)])
r2[region$variant_id == lead] <- 1
bin <- cut(r2, breaks = c(-0.01, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.01), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
colours <- c("#0072B2", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00")
shapes <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 16)
png(guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png"), width = 1400, height = 900, res = 150)
plot(region$base_pair_location / 1e6, -log10(region$p_value), col = ifelse(is.na(bin), "#666666", colours[bin]),
  pch = ifelse(is.na(bin), 8, shapes[bin]), xlab = "GRCh38 chromosome 9 position (Mb)", ylab = "-log10(p)", main = "L2: association and LD to the lead")
abline(h = -log10(5e-8), lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("r2: 0 to 0.2", "0.2 to 0.4", "0.4 to 0.6", "0.6 to 0.8", "0.8 to 1", "LD unavailable"),
  pch = c(shapes, 8), col = c(colours, "#666666"), cex = 0.8)
invisible(dev.off())
cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png"), "\n", sep = "")
stopifnot(sum(region$p_value < 5e-8) == 4L)
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "7.6", c(paste0(report, ".vcor"), guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png")), parent = "6.8")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --chr 9 --from-bp 95926973 --to-bp 96926973 --r2-unphased --ld-snp 9:96426973:A:G --ld-window-kb 500 --ld-window-r2 0 --out results/guided/s7-6_ld --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--chr 9`, `--from-bp` and `--to-bp` define an interval of one megabase on chromosome 9 in GRCh38. `--r2-unphased` reports the squared correlation of the genotype dosages. `--ld-snp` makes the lead variant the first member of every pair. `--ld-window-kb 500` limits the distance from the lead to 500 kilobases. `--ld-window-r2 0` keeps low correlations as well as high ones; without it, points with low LD could disappear from the report. `--out`, threads and memory have the meanings given earlier.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

L2 has four genome-wide significant variants. The plot shows LD by both symbol and colour. If an LD value is missing, the legend says "LD unavailable". The value is not silently set to zero. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

```{r s7-6_expected_figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="Four L2 variants pass the genome-wide threshold; symbol and colour indicate LD with the chromosome 9 lead."}
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error. Check the input file that R names and the previous step. Keep the command and the messages from the console. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Does the highest point always identify the causal variant?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The lead variant is the strongest association among the sites that we tested. It may only mark a cause that we did not measure.

</details>

### Files created

`s7-6_ld.vcor`, `s7-6_regional.png` and the regional analysis checkpoint.

## 7.7 Compare without PCs and without QC {#step-7-7}

### What we do

Compare the main analysis, which we planned in advance, with two analyses that we deliberately make weaker.

### Why

In the first comparison, we leave out the [PCs](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc). PCs are the numbers that summarise ancestry. We keep the same cleaned cohort and the same [covariates](../docs/glossary.md#covariate), age and sex. This shows the effect of the PC adjustment alone.

In the second comparison, we start from the state saved at module 2. It has the case and control labels and the corrected strands. We use no sample [QC](../docs/glossary.md#qc), no variant QC and no PCs. This comparison changes the samples and the variants as well as the QC. We cannot give its differences to one single cause. The label "no QC" does not mean that we undid the strand correction or the case and control labels. When you interpret the differences, compare the shared variants and the number of samples for each variant.

### You need

The state from step 5.7, the state from step 2.8, the summary statistics file from step 6.8 for the main analysis, the covariates and the original sample information. The two comparison scans are new PLINK reports. R puts them into the same standard columns in memory. In this way, all three analyses are summarised in the same way.

### Command

```{r s7-7}
no_pc <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "no_pcs")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", no_pc))
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)
all_covar <- metadata[c("FID", "IID", "Age")]; names(all_covar)[1] <- "#FID"
all_file <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "all_ages.tsv"); guided_write(all_covar, all_file)
no_qc <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "no_qc_no_pcs")
baseline <- guided_path(cfg, "2.8")
if (!file.exists(paste0(baseline, ".pgen"))) baseline <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "checkpoints", "2.8", "state")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", baseline, "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", all_file,
  "--covar-name", "Age", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", no_qc))
main <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
a <- guided_standardise_scan(guided_association(no_pc))
b <- guided_standardise_scan(guided_association(no_qc))
k <- match(main$variant_id, a$variant_id)
stopifnot(!anyNA(k), all(main$n == a$n[k]))
autosomal_p <- function(x) x$p_value[x$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)]
summarise <- function(x) c(finite_tests = sum(valid_p(x$p_value)), hits = sum(x$p_value[valid_p(x$p_value)] < 5e-8),
  lambda = lambda_gc(autosomal_p(x)))
comparison <- rbind(main = summarise(main), no_PCs = summarise(a), no_sample_or_variant_QC_no_PCs = summarise(b))
print(comparison)
stopifnot(comparison[2, "hits"] == 15L, comparison[3, "hits"] == 19L)
guided_write(data.frame(model = rownames(comparison), comparison, row.names = NULL), guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"))
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "qq_comparison.png"), function() {
  par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
  plotted <- list(autosomal_p(main), autosomal_p(a), autosomal_p(b))
  limits <- c(0, max(-log10(unlist(plotted))))
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(main), "QC + ten PCs", ylim = limits)
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(a), "QC, no PCs", ylim = limits)
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(b), "No sample/variant QC, no PCs", ylim = limits)
}, width = 2100, height = 750)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --maf 0.01 --covar results/guided/s6-3_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age --covar-variance-standardize --glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback --out results/guided/s7-7_no_pcs --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s2-8_state --maf 0.01 --covar results/guided/s7-7_all_ages.tsv --covar-name Age --covar-variance-standardize --glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback --out results/guided/s7-7_no_qc_no_pcs --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback` fits the association model with the recorded sex, reports only the genetic tests and uses Firth correction when needed. `--covar` loads the covariate table, which is matched by sample ID. `--covar-variance-standardize` rescales numerical covariates so the fitting is stable. `--covar-name Age` keeps only age and so leaves out the PCs on purpose. The first call keeps the cleaned cohort. The second call changes `--pfile` to the state before QC and uses the ages of all wells. `--maf 0.01` stays as a rule for which variants are tested, also in the comparison without QC. `--out` keeps the outputs apart; threads and memory are unchanged.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Main analysis: 236,815 tests, eight hits, lambda about 1.016. Without PCs after QC: 236,815 tests, 15 hits, lambda about 1.546. Without sample or variant QC and without PCs: 239,647 tests, 19 hits, lambda about 1.655. The extra peaks do not show that worse QC finds more true causes.

The tested PLINK version is set in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: the executable chunks, the comparisons with the expected results and the final plot checks passed on Windows.

## 7.8 Final summary and reporting {#step-7-8}

### What we do

Write a clear summary of the whole simulated main path. Save the final results and figures so that others can check them.

### Why

A report must link the study design, the QC decisions, the model, the effect sizes, the uncertainty and the figures. Include the genome build, the software versions, the numbers of samples, the exclusions, the PCs, the tested allele and the threshold. Report the [odds ratio](../docs/glossary.md#or) and its 95% [confidence interval](../docs/glossary.md#ci) for each lead variant. The interval shows how uncertain the estimate is.

Keep two differences clear. An association that we observed is not a proof of a cause. A signal that we simulated for teaching is not a biological discovery. A result that is not significant can come from low [statistical power](../docs/glossary.md#statistical-power), which is the chance to detect an effect of a given size in this study. Keep a record that others can repeat, but do not publish data about single people.

### You need

Modules 0 to 6, checked. Also the summary statistics file from step 6.8 and the figures and comparisons from steps 7.1 to 7.7.

### Command

```{r s7-8}
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))
comparison <- read.delim(guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"))
clumps <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump"), ".clumps"))
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
lead <- stats[match(clumps$ID, stats$variant_id), c("chromosome", "base_pair_location", "variant_id", "effect_allele", "odds_ratio", "beta", "standard_error", "p_value", "n")]
lead$ci_low <- exp(lead$beta - 1.96 * lead$standard_error)
lead$ci_high <- exp(lead$beta + 1.96 * lead$standard_error)
guided_write(lead, guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "leads.tsv"))
summary <- c("# Simulated GWAS: main-path summary", "", "Genome assembly: GRCh38. Simulated data, seed 20261111.",
  paste("Software:", paste(cfg$version, collapse = "; ")),
  "Initial: 2,016 measured wells, 2,000 people, 299,523 variant entries.",
  paste("Final cohort:", nrow(psam), "samples; cases:", sum(psam$Disease == "2"), "; controls:", sum(psam$Disease == "1")),
  "After QC: 238,513 variants; 236,815 finite additive association tests.",
  "Model: additive logistic regression, adjusted for age, recorded sex and ten within-cohort PCs; Firth fallback enabled.",
  "Eight variants pass p < 5e-8 in three LD clumps. Autosomal lambda is approximately 1.016.",
  "Report the effect allele, odds ratio, 95% interval, p-value and per-variant sample count n from s7-8_leads.tsv.",
  "Interpretation: the three strong simulated regions are recovered; the moderate region is subthreshold. No causal gene is established.",
  "Sensitivity: omitting PCs increases lambda to approximately 1.546; omitting sample/variant QC as well gives approximately 1.655.",
  "Limitations: simulated design, selected array sites, finite power, provisional imported REF labels, study-specific QC and ancestry rules.",
  "Three named ancestry markers left at HWE step 4.4; comparisons must not pretend they survived to module 5.",
  "Figures: s7-1_qq.png, s7-3_manhattan.png, s7-6_regional.png and s7-7_qq_comparison.png.",
  "No biological discovery or clinical recommendation follows from this simulation.")
writeLines(summary, guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "summary.md"), useBytes = TRUE)
files <- c(guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "summary.md"), guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "leads.tsv"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.1", "qq.png"), guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png"), guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "qq_comparison.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump"), ".clumps"),
  file.path(cfg$out, "step_counts.tsv"), file.path(cfg$out, "software_versions.txt"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "7.8", files, parent = "6.8")
check_step("7.8", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
cat(paste(summary, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
```

### Quick check

What more evidence would we need before we call a simulated association a biological discovery?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

We would need real data that are handled under proper rules, [replication](../docs/glossary.md#replication) in independent data and suitable biological evidence. This simulation gives none of these.

## Module 7 recap {#module-7-recap}

- You drew a QQ plot and calculated an autosomal lambda of approximately 1.016.
- You drew a Manhattan plot. Eight variants are below 5e-8, in three regions on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12.
- You compared thresholds: 5e-8 for the usual rule and approximately 2.11e-7 from Bonferroni for 236,815 tests.
- You grouped the eight variants into three clumps and looked at the L2 region on chromosome 9.
- Without PCs the lambda rose to about 1.546, and without sample or variant QC as well it rose to about 1.655.
- You wrote a final summary and a table of the lead variants.

**Next:** this is the last module of the main path. You can now report your findings, with their limits. Modules A (imputation) and B (mixed models) are optional extras and are not part of the main path.
